idiom_name: frozen abstract interface + adapter over the new core
implementation_notes: The window is a class that implements the legacy interface exactly as declared - same signatures, same const-ness, same error and exception contract - and delegates every call to the modernized core, with the field mapping confined to one translation unit; [[deprecated]] marks the frozen interface so new code cannot adopt it by accident. Where the legacy consumer is a binary or is not a C++ program, the contract is the C ABI rather than the C++ signature, and the window becomes an extern "C" boundary with opaque handles, because language linkage pins calling convention and name mangling while C++ object layout does not stay stable across toolchains. The hand-written adapter is still justified when the old interface must be frozen verbatim; when the consumer can be rebuilt, deriving both shapes from one schema is cheaper than maintaining the mapping by hand.
pitfalls: Inline functions, templates and default arguments live in the frozen header, so they are part of the contract: changing one silently changes behaviour for consumers you cannot rebuild.
Exception and RTTI settings must match the legacy build; letting an exception cross a differently configured boundary (or a C frame) is undefined behaviour.
std::string and containers in the interface pin allocator and ABI together: if the caller is a C module, hand back opaque handles and plain buffers instead.

variants.name: extern "C" ABI shim for binary or foreign-language consumers
variants.implementation_notes: When the legacy consumer is a binary or is written in another language, the contract is the C ABI, not the C++ signature: export the old symbols inside extern "C" so calling convention and name mangling are pinned by the standard's language linkage, hand back opaque handles instead of C++ objects, and translate errors into numeric codes at the boundary. cppreference states what that buys - language linkage encapsulates 'the requirements necessary to link with a program unit written in another programming language: calling convention, name mangling' - and, by the same token, what is left outside the standard: struct layout and exceptions across the boundary remain the shim's responsibility. Choose this variant when old binaries must keep linking; choose the interface adapter when the consumer is rebuilt in C++ anyway.
pitfalls: Every compiler and standard-library version is a different C++ ABI; a shim built against the wrong toolchain undermines its own friendly C surface.
Passing exceptions or non-POD types through the C boundary is undefined: catch inside the shim and map to the legacy error codes.
